**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — A planned humanitarian release of hostages held by Colombia's largest guerrilla group has descended into confusion and controversy, leaving families of the captives in an agonizing limbo after DNA test results contradicted claims made by the rebel organization.

## Background on the Case

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) had announced plans to unilaterally release several long-held hostages, including Clara Rojas, a former vice-presidential candidate who was kidnapped alongside presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt in 2002, and Consuelo González de Perdomo, a former congresswoman.

The case gained international attention due to a deeply emotional element: Rojas was reported to have given birth to a son, Emmanuel, during her years in captivity in the jungle. FARC claimed the child had been held by a peasant family for years before being handed over to Colombian child welfare authorities under a different identity, and that the boy would be reunited with his mother as part of the release operation.

## The Failed Release Operation

International intermediaries, including Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez and representatives from Argentina, France, and the International Committee of the Red Cross, mobilized to facilitate the release. Aircraft and diplomatic personnel were positioned to retrieve the hostages from the Colombian jungle.

However, the operation collapsed when FARC failed to produce the hostages at the agreed-upon location and time. The rebel group cited military operations by Colombian armed forces in the area as the reason the handover could not proceed safely, though Colombian President Álvaro Uribe's government disputed this characterization, accusing FARC of manufacturing excuses.

Perhaps the most dramatic turn in the saga came when Colombian authorities revealed that a young boy already in state custody—believed by many to be Emmanuel—had, in fact, been confirmed through DNA testing to be Clara Rojas's son.

This revelation proved deeply embarrassing for FARC, which had claimed for years that the child remained with a peasant family in guerrilla-controlled territory. It emerged that Emmanuel had actually been taken into the custody of Colombia's Institute of Family Welfare (ICBF) years earlier, after the peasant family who had been caring for him brought him to a hospital and he was subsequently placed into the child welfare system—all without FARC's apparent knowledge of his whereabouts.

The Colombian government seized on this discovery as evidence of FARC's disorganization and dishonesty, with President Uribe stating that the rebels had "lied" about maintaining custody of the child they had used as a bargaining chip in negotiations.

## Reactions and Implications

Family members of Rojas expressed a mixture of relief and anguish upon learning of Emmanuel's true circumstances—relieved the child was safe and had been receiving care, but distressed by years of uncertainty and the FARC's apparent deception.

International mediators expressed frustration at the collapsed operation, with Chávez—who had positioned himself as a key figure in hostage negotiations—voicing displeasure at both FARC's handling of the situation and the Colombian government's military posture in the region.

Human rights advocates noted the case underscored the broader humanitarian crisis facing hundreds of hostages still held by FARC, many for years, in Colombia's ongoing internal conflict. Advocacy groups renewed calls for a more comprehensive humanitarian exchange agreement between the government and the rebel group.

## What's Next

Colombian officials indicated that arrangements would be made for Rojas and González to eventually be reunited with their families once new logistics for their release could be established. Meanwhile, the fate of Emmanuel became a focal point for renewed negotiations, with international pressure mounting on both FARC and the Colombian government to prioritize the child's reunification with his mother.

The episode highlighted the extraordinary complexity and emotional toll of Colombia's decades-long conflict, where hostages have become both human beings caught in tragic circumstances and pawns in a broader political and military struggle.

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — A highly anticipated New Year's Eve release of three hostages held by Colombia's largest rebel group collapsed in confusion and recrimination, exposing an embarrassing truth: the guerrillas no longer had custody of the child they had promised to hand over.

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known by its Spanish acronym FARC, had pledged to release former congresswoman Clara Rojas, former legislator Consuelo González de Perdomo, and Rojas's young son, Emmanuel, born in captivity, as part of a humanitarian gesture brokered with the help of Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez. Helicopters from Venezuela and the International Committee of the Red Cross stood by in the Colombian jungle for days awaiting coordinates from the rebels. None came.

Colombian officials then delivered a stunning disclosure: a boy matching Emmanuel's description had been living in state protective custody for more than two years, placed there under a different name after being taken, ill and malnourished, to a rural hospital by a peasant family in 2005. The FARC, it turned out, had lost track of the child it claimed to be holding.

## A Race to Confirm an Identity

The revelation triggered an urgent effort by Colombia's child welfare agency, the ICBF, and government forensic laboratories to determine whether the boy in custody — registered under the name given by the family that brought him in — was in fact Emmanuel.

Investigators compared genetic samples from the child with those of Clara Rojas's relatives, since Rojas herself remained in rebel hands in the southern jungles. Officials said they moved quickly, aware that a mistaken identification, in either direction, would be a devastating blow to a fragile release process already strained by mutual distrust between the government of President Álvaro Uribe and the FARC's negotiators.

Within days, laboratory results confirmed what many officials had begun to suspect: the boy was indeed Emmanuel, Clara Rojas's son, conceived and born inside a FARC camp under conditions his mother has since described as harrowing. The confirmation resolved one mystery even as it deepened another — how a rebel force that had held the child for roughly the first ten months of his life had failed to prevent, or even register, his transfer into state hands.

## A Long War, and a Familiar Tactic

The episode is only the latest turn in a kidnapping saga that has come to symbolize the FARC's decades-long insurgency. Founded in 1964 as the armed wing of Colombia's Communist Party, the FARC grew from a small peasant self-defense movement into Latin America's most enduring guerrilla army, at its peak fielding an estimated 18,000 fighters and controlling swaths of Colombian territory roughly the size of Switzerland.

Financed increasingly through cocaine trafficking, extortion, and ransom kidnappings, the group has for years used high-profile hostages as bargaining chips, seeking the exchange of captured rebels held in Colombian prisons. Clara Rojas was among the highest-value hostages: she was kidnapped in February 2002 alongside Ingrid Betancourt, a French-Colombian presidential candidate, while the two campaigned in FARC-dominated territory. Betancourt remains among dozens of hostages the rebels continue to hold, along with three American defense contractors whose surveillance plane crashed in rebel territory in 2003, and numerous Colombian police officers and soldiers, some held for over a decade.

Human rights groups estimate the FARC has held thousands of hostages over the course of the conflict, ranging from politicians and security forces to ordinary citizens seized for ransom. Conditions in jungle camps have been described by former captives as brutal — long marches in chains, tropical disease, and prolonged isolation. Rojas has said she was separated from her infant son for extended periods and that his birth, delivered without proper medical care, left him with health complications that FARC captors were ill-equipped to treat, prompting his transfer to a rural family and, ultimately, state custody.

## Diplomacy Amid Distrust

The attempted New Year's release had been engineered as a unilateral humanitarian gesture, part of a broader mediation effort led by Chávez at the invitation of the Colombian government, which had granted him a limited role reaching out to the rebel leadership. The plan called for coordinates to be provided to the Red Cross for a jungle pickup, mirroring protocols used in past prisoner exchanges.

When the FARC failed to produce the child — and, government officials said, appeared genuinely unaware of his whereabouts — the operation was thrown into disarray. Bogotá alternated between accusing the rebels of a publicity stunt and acknowledging that the mishap likely reflected a genuine breakdown in the FARC's internal command and control, a group whose secretariat and negotiators are often separated by hundreds of miles of jungle and years of intermittent contact with regional field commanders.

Uribe's government, which had approached the Chávez-led mediation with open skepticism, seized on the episode as evidence of the rebels' disorganization, while also moving to ensure the botched handover would not derail the release of the two women.

## Release Without the Child

Roughly ten days after the failed New Year's attempt, Rojas and González de Perdomo were flown out of the jungle in a Venezuelan-marked helicopter and handed to the Red Cross, ending years of captivity. Emmanuel, already confirmed through DNA analysis to be in government custody, was not part of that handover — he had, in effect, already been "released" without either side realizing it.

Colombian officials say the boy will be reunited with his mother following medical and psychological evaluation, a reunion Rojas has said she has awaited since she last saw her son as an infant.

The episode has renewed international pressure on the FARC to release its remaining hostages, including Betancourt and the American contractors, and has raised fresh questions about the rebel group's capacity to manage a captive population increasingly dispersed across remote camps as the group has come under sustained military pressure from Colombian security forces. Analysts say the confusion surrounding Emmanuel may complicate future negotiations, as government officials voice skepticism about the FARC's ability to reliably account for the hostages it claims to hold.

For now, officials in Bogotá say the DNA results have closed one chapter of the story even as the larger conflict, and the fate of the FARC's remaining captives, continues.
